In these circumstances, the Wine Australia Act is not contravened and so a section 42(b) ground for rejection should not be raised."}],"answer":"A slight spelling change is not an automatic way around the objection. That is an inference from the Manual’s express coverage of marks that “resemble” a protected Wine Register entry, not just identical marks, where the application claims relevant Class 33 grape products. I cannot say whether your particular brand would be registered. The supplied Manual practice identifies these considerations:

• Protected wine terms: resemblance to a Wine Register entry may indicate that use would contravene the Wine Australia Act unless it accords with the entry’s conditions. The Manual provides for consent to a condition of registration restricting use accordingly; it says this allows the section 42 objection to be withdrawn. [2–3]

• Deception or confusion: separately, examiners should consider section 43 where a geographic reference conveys a connotation likely to deceive or confuse consumers in relation to the claimed goods or services—even if the reference is not a recognised geographical indication. [4]

• Context: the Manual says a section 42(b) objection should not be raised where the context means the protected term does not actually refer to the Wine Register term. This is a contextual distinction, not a stated spelling-change exception. [5]
